title: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic court former Trump AI advisor to run private frontier-model regulator
subtitle: The proposed Frontier AI Standards Agency, modeled on Wall Street's FINRA, would set voluntary safety standards for the three companies' own models — without government oversight.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic have approached Sriram Krishnan — the former Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence in the second Trump administration — to lead a self-regulator tentatively called the Frontier AI Standards Agency, reports surfaced this week said. The proposed body is modeled on FINRA, the private organization that oversees U.S. broker-dealers. Its pillars, as described so far, include shared technical evaluations, pre-release audits, independent testing frameworks and standardized safety protocols. Target launch: late 2026 or early 2027.

The irony is doing a lot of work. Krishnan spent his time in office arguing that Washington should not build an FDA for AI — that a centralized agency requiring 'a team of lawyers before you can get a model out' would 'put sand in the gears of the AI revolution.' Now the three largest frontier labs want to build exactly that agency themselves, and want him to run it. That configuration is not accidental. If you cannot stop Washington from eventually setting rules, the next-best position is to define what compliance already looks like — with a friendly executive at the top and your own testing framework as the reference standard.

This is a familiar pattern in industries where regulation is inevitable but not yet finalized. Wall Street's FINRA is the textbook example, and the model has real strengths: technical expertise concentrated inside the industry, faster rule-making cycles than a federal agency, and enforcement muscle backed by member firms. It also has textbook weaknesses. Self-regulators tend to protect incumbents, define 'safety' in ways that raise the cost of entry for smaller labs, and negotiate with themselves in rooms the public cannot enter. Whether the Frontier AI Standards Agency ends up closer to FINRA or closer to a shared marketing arm depends almost entirely on how independent its testing is from the labs paying for it.

Takeaway for learners: 'AI governance' is not one field. It has at least three sub-fields — capabilities evaluation, deployment policy, and the political economy of who writes the rules — and they hire different people. If policy work interests you, the political-economy question is the least crowded and arguably the most important right now. Read the FINRA history, read the EU AI Act debates, and pay attention to who is being courted for which chair.
